sections.h2: Sugar Land city tax rate for 2026
sections.html:
For Tax Year 2026 the adopted city rate is $0.371116 per $100 of taxable value. It is only the city's slice of a Sugar Land bill. The school district, Fort Bend County and any MUD or LID levy sit on top of it, and your tax bill shows which ones apply to your house.

Two pieces make it up: $0.220157 for maintenance and operations, and $0.150959 for debt service, which pays back borrowing for city projects. The city's share is about 21 percent of the residential bill in Fort Bend ISD and 19 percent in Lamar CISD, before any MUD or LID taxes.

Both Tax Year 2025 and Tax Year 2026 brought a small increase.

For 2026 the no-new-revenue rate is $0.355381 and the voter-approval rate is $0.381586. The voter-approval rate is the ceiling the city cannot pass without a vote. The median homestead's estimated annual city bill is $1,371 for 2026, against $1,312 the prior year.

Each September, council votes on the rate after approving the budget and holding a public hearing. The city has until 60 days after it gets the certified tax roll, or September 30, whichever is later. Appraised values are certified by July 25, so the rate cannot be final until that roll is in.

Two benchmarks frame the vote. At the no-new-revenue rate, existing property brings in the same money as last year. The voter-approval rate is the highest the city can set without an election, and it covers debt service plus a 3.5 percent increase in maintenance and operations revenue.

A taxpayer impact statement from the city shows, for 2026, a $4.90 monthly impact for the median homestead, and budgeted property tax revenue of $81,205,666 for FY2027.

City leaders call the rate one of the lowest in the state for a city this size. Since 1993 the rate has dropped from 50 cents to 35 cents per $100, a change the city credits to economic development and sales tax growth, while the city homestead exemption rose from 1 percent to 15 percent.

In 17 years the average home value has risen about 4.6 percent a year, while the average city tax bill rose about 4.0 percent a year. Average home value is $540,358 for Tax Year 2026 against $529,032 for 2025, with an average homestead exemption of $81,054. These are citywide averages, so lean on your own appraisal notice and bill when pricing the house.

The city homestead exemption is 15 percent of assessed value, plus $70,000 for owners over 65 and $70,000 for disabled persons. Someone who is both over 65 and disabled gets just one. A disabled veteran should ask the Fort Bend Central Appraisal District about the amount.

School districts have their own exemptions. The state-required school homestead exemption is $140,000, with another $60,000 for seniors and disabled owners. Owners who are older or disabled also receive a school tax ceiling, which freezes the school bill near what it was when they first qualified.

  • You must own the house and live in it as your main home, and claim no other homestead anywhere.
  • If you never filed, a buyer who closes after New Year's Day can still file for the remainder of that tax year.
  • File with the appraisal district rather than city hall.

sections.h2: Who values your house and who collects
sections.html:
Two county offices handle your bill. The Fort Bend Central Appraisal District decides what the house is worth. The Fort Bend County Tax Assessor-Collector sends the bill and takes payment for the city by contract. Take valuation and exemption questions to the appraisal district.

The appraisal district's office is at 2801 B F Terry Blvd, Rosenberg, TX 77471, phone 281-344-8623. To apply for an exemption, send a copy of your Texas driver's license or DPS ID, and make sure the address on it matches the property address.

Value is fixed as of January 1. Homestead notices arrive around April 1, most protests are due by mid-May, and the records are approved in July. If you think the value is wrong, you must object within that window.

The target is January 31, and an open bill on February 1 is delinquent. When a bill is mailed after January 10, the cutoff slides to the first day of a later month that leaves 21 days or more. Owners who are seniors or disabled may pay in four installments.

  • On February 1 a 6 percent penalty and 1 percent interest attach.
  • Each month adds more penalty, reaching 12 percent on July 1.
  • Nothing caps the interest, and a collection lawyer may tack on up to 20 percent.

Each year's lien takes hold on January 1, and whoever owned the house that day may be sued for the bill even after selling. That is why the closing agent orders a tax certificate and deducts what is owed from your funds.

A bill left unpaid goes through notices, a possible payment plan and eventually a lawsuit that adds costs. In the end a taxing unit can foreclose and auction the house.

Are back taxes pushing you to sell? Phone the Fort Bend County Tax Assessor-Collector for a payoff number first, then price the house. Armed with that, you can set a listing, a private sale and a cash offer side by side. Ask the office too whether penalty and interest can be waived if you pay soon after learning the bill is late, since that sometimes happens.

sections.h2: What to gather before you sell
sections.html:
Pull out your newest tax bill. It lists every taxing unit, any MUD or LID charge, and whether an exemption sits on the account. Next get a payoff number from the county tax office, and ask the title company which amounts it will collect at closing.

Bring the bill when you meet any buyer or agent. It answers most of their first questions and shows that you know what you owe.

Your exemptions need a look too. The homestead exemption belongs to the owner who claimed it and stops with the sale, so the buyer must file separately. Neither a cash purchase nor a listing changes this, and the next owner's bill is figured without your savings.

Selling for cash skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting. The title search and tax payoff then set the closing date, and a current account with a clean deed can mean a short wait.

faqs.q: What is the 2026 city tax rate in Sugar Land?
faqs.a: The adopted city rate is $0.371116 per $100 of taxable value. School, county and any MUD or LID rates come on top.

faqs.q: Does Sugar Land give a homestead exemption?
faqs.a: Yes: 15 percent of assessed value, plus $70,000 for owners over 65 or $70,000 for disabled persons, one of the two at most. File with the Fort Bend Central Appraisal District.

faqs.q: Who gets my Sugar Land tax payment?
faqs.a: The Fort Bend County Tax Assessor-Collector, which collects for the city by contract. Value and exemption questions go to the appraisal district.

faqs.q: When does a Sugar Land bill go delinquent?
faqs.a: After January 31. February 1 adds a 6 percent penalty plus 1 percent interest.

faqs.q: Can I sell if I owe taxes on my Sugar Land house?
faqs.a: Yes. The closing agent pays the balance with your proceeds, so get a payoff figure from the county tax office first.
